newsitem.title: USA: SOCCER-AMBITIOUS WOMEN'S WORLD CUP PLANNED FOR 1999.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-AMBITIOUS WOMEN'S WORLD CUP PLANNED FOR 1999.

text.p: U.S. soccer organisers are planning an ambitious 1999 Women's World Cup that will dwarf the previous two stagings of the event, tournament officials said Wednesday.

"The first one in China was sort of hidden away in China and in Sweden it was purposefully done very small and low-key," U.S. Soccer president Alan Rothenberg said of the first two Women's World Cups, held in 1991 and 1995.
"This time we are going for it," Rothenberg said at a news conference to introduce members of the organising committee including former Olympic gold medalist swimmer Donna de Varona as chairwoman.
"We are going to make this the biggest women's sports tournament in our lifetime," said Rothenberg, who was the head of the men's World Cup held in the United States in 1994.
The Women's World Cup is scheduled for June 20-July 7. Sixteen teams will play, with only the host U.S. team, the 1991 champions, assured of a spot. Defending champions Norway will have to qualify.
When the United States first won the right to stage the event, organisers envisioned a small tournament played in four cities all located in the American Northeast.
"Our thinking was to hold a small event and have a nice little soccer tournament," said Hank Steinbrecher, executive director of U.S. Soccer.
According to Rothenberg, planners originally envisaged using stadiums of no more than 15,000 capacity.

But after seeing the rousing success of women's soccer in last year's Olympic Games in Atlanta, where a crowd of 76,489 watched the United States beat China in the gold medal game, organisers began thinking much bigger.
"We really want to move this from being a small regional tournament to becoming an international, large-scale tournament," said Rothenberg.

"We want to give it the surroundings it deserve," he added. "We want major stadiums. I would venture to say that every stadium that was in used in 1994 (World Cup) with the possible exception of the (Detroit) Silverdome would be in the hunt."
Twenty cities are expected to bid to hold games with the final six or seven to be announced later this year.
Comparisions to the 1994 World Cup will be made but this tournament will have its own lasting significance, said Rothenberg.
"In terms of impact it could be greater, because World Cup was a big challenge, but at the same time it had a history," he said. "Here in many ways there is no history."
